def: To succeed in doing or completing something.
ex: She managed to accomplish all her weekly goals before Friday.
nat: What do you hope to accomplish this year?

mis.bad: I accomplished to finish early.
mis.good: I managed to finish early.
mis.why: Use "accomplish + noun" (a goal, a task), not "to + verb".

def: Familiar with something so that it seems normal or usual.
ex: It takes a few weeks to get accustomed to driving on the left.
nat: I am not accustomed to waking up at five.

mis.bad: I am accustomed with the noise.
mis.good: I am accustomed to the noise.

def: To buy or obtain an asset, object, or skill for oneself.
ex: You acquire fluency through daily listening and speaking practice.
nat: The company acquired a smaller competitor last year.

mis.bad: I acquired a cold yesterday.
mis.good: I caught a cold yesterday.
mis.why: Use "acquire" for skills, habits, or assets; use "catch" for a cold.

def: Next to or adjoining something else.
ex: Our meeting room is adjacent to the main reception desk.
nat: They booked two adjacent seats on the flight.

mis.bad: The park is adjacent with the station.
mis.good: The park is adjacent to the station.

def: To regard with respect or warm approval.
ex: I really admire how calm she stays during stressful incidents.
nat: We stopped at the viewpoint to admire the mountain scenery.

mis.bad: I admire her by her patience.
mis.good: I admire her for her patience.

def: Preventing success or development; harmful or unfavorable.
ex: The flight was delayed due to adverse weather conditions over the Atlantic.
nat: The medication had no adverse side effects.

mis.bad: He had an averse reaction to the news.
mis.good: He had an adverse impact / felt averse to the idea.
mis.why: "Adverse" describes conditions/effects; "averse" describes a person's reluctance.

def: Having a great deal of money; wealthy.
ex: The cafe opened in an affluent neighborhood near the financial district.
nat: Demand for organic food grew fastest among affluent households.

mis.bad: He is very affluent in English.
mis.good: He is very fluent in English.
mis.why: "Affluent" means rich; "fluent" means speaking a language smoothly.

def: To make a problem, injury, or offense worse or more serious.
ex: Skipping sleep will only aggravate your headache.
nat: Constant interruptions aggravate stress across the whole team.

mis.bad: The noise aggravated to me.
mis.good: The noise aggravated me.

def: Able to move quickly and easily, or adapt rapidly to change.
ex: Small teams stay agile because they can decide without five layers of approval.
nat: Cats are remarkably agile climbers.

mis.bad: We use a very agilely process.
mis.good: We use a very agile process.

def: An illness, typically a minor one.
ex: Ginger tea is a traditional home remedy for minor stomach ailments.
nat: The clinic treats common seasonal ailments without an appointment.

mis.bad: He died of a minor ailment.
mis.good: He recovered from a minor ailment.
mis.why: An "ailment" is usually mild or chronic, not fatal.

def: Worrying or disturbing.
ex: Error rates have been climbing at an alarming pace since noon.
nat: The report revealed an alarming drop in freshwater reserves.

mis.bad: I felt very alarming about the news.
mis.good: I felt very alarmed by the news.
mis.why: Use "-ing" for what causes the feeling ("alarming news") and "-ed" for how a person feels ("alarmed").

def: To make someone feel isolated or estranged.
ex: Forcing sudden changes without explanation can alienate loyal users.
nat: His harsh tone alienated several colleagues.

mis.bad: He alienated from his friends.
mis.good: He alienated his friends / felt alienated from them.

def: To claim or assert that someone has done something illegal or wrong, typically without proof.
ex: The former employee alleged that safety reports had been altered.
nat: The report alleges widespread billing errors.

mis.bad: He alleged me of stealing.
mis.good: He accused me of stealing / alleged that I had stolen.

def: To make suffering, deficiency, or a problem less severe.
ex: Better documentation will help alleviate the burden on senior engineers.
nat: Ibuprofen can quickly alleviate mild fever and pain.

mis.bad: This medicine alleviates from the pain.
mis.good: This medicine alleviates the pain.

def: A union or association formed for mutual benefit, especially between countries or organizations.
ex: The two airlines formed an alliance to share routes across Europe.
nat: A strong alliance between design and engineering speeds up delivery.

mis.bad: They made an alliance against the competitor.
mis.good: They formed an alliance with each other.

def: To give or apportion something to someone as a share or task.
ex: Each speaker was allotted exactly ten minutes for the presentation.
nat: We used all the allotted budget before December.

mis.bad: They allotted 10 minutes to me speak.
mis.good: They allotted me 10 minutes to speak.

def: To change or cause to change in character or composition, typically slightly.
ex: Do not alter the database schema without running a migration script.
nat: Bad weather forced us to alter our travel route.

mis.bad: We altered about the schedule.
mis.good: We altered the schedule.

def: To occur in turn repeatedly.
ex: Try to alternate between passive listening and active speaking exercises.
nat: The team members alternate on-call shifts every Monday.

mis.bad: We alternate with each other doing it.
mis.good: We alternate doing it / take turns doing it.
mis.why: Use "alternate between A and B" or "alternate + -ing".

def: To gather together or accumulate a large amount of something over time.
ex: Over ten years, the company amassed millions of customer support logs.
nat: She amassed a small fortune through early index investing.

mis.bad: He amassed many knowledges.
mis.good: He amassed a lot of knowledge.
mis.why: "Knowledge" is uncountable; use "a lot of knowledge".

def: Enough or more than enough; plentiful.
ex: Leave ample time to clear airport security during holiday weekends.
nat: The apartment has ample storage space for a family of three.

mis.bad: We have ample of time.
mis.good: We have ample time.

def: To increase the volume, strength, or effect of something.
ex: Social media algorithms tend to amplify emotional headlines.
nat: A good microphone will amplify your voice clearly without background hum.

mis.bad: The speaker amplified up the sound.
mis.good: The speaker amplified the sound.

def: Comparable in certain respects, typically in a way that makes clearer the nature of the things compared.
ex: A firewall is analogous to a security guard checking badges at the door.
nat: The human brain is often described as analogous to a complex network.

mis.bad: This system is analogous with an airport.
mis.good: This system is analogous to an airport.

def: To secure firmly in position, or provide a stable reference point.
ex: Try to anchor your study habit to an existing morning routine like coffee.
nat: A strong opening story can anchor the entire presentation.

mis.bad: We anchored the habit on coffee.
mis.good: We anchored the habit to coffee.

def: A short amusing or interesting story about a real incident or person.
ex: He opened his talk with a funny anecdote about his first day as an intern.
nat: Data matters, but a single vivid anecdote often convinces the room.

mis.bad: Let me tell you an anecdote joke.
mis.good: Let me tell you a funny anecdote.
mis.why: In English, "anecdote" means a short real-life story, not a joke ("joke").

def: To destroy utterly; obliterate.
ex: One careless drop-table command could annihilate months of test data.
nat: The home team annihilated their rivals five to zero.

mis.bad: The fire annihilated down the building.
mis.good: The fire completely destroyed the building.

def: To add notes to a text or diagram giving explanation or comment.
ex: Please annotate the screenshots so the designer knows which button to move.
nat: Reviewers often annotate PDF contracts before signing.

mis.bad: I annotated on the PDF.
mis.good: I annotated the PDF.

def: To cause someone to become hostile or unfriendly.
ex: Sending aggressive reminder emails will only antagonize late-paying clients.
nat: Try not to antagonize the interviewer if they challenge your answer.

mis.bad: He antagonized with his boss.
mis.good: He antagonized his boss.

def: Lack of interest, enthusiasm, or concern.
ex: Voter apathy reached a record high during the local elections.
nat: Unrealistic targets often create apathy instead of motivation.

mis.bad: There is much apathy from the team.
mis.good: There is widespread apathy in the team.
mis.why: Say "apathy among/in [a group]" or "apathy toward [a topic]".

def: Causing shock or dismay; horrific or very bad.
ex: The customer service at that airport counter was truly appalling.
nat: Workers were forced to operate in appalling safety conditions.

mis.bad: I was appalling by the quality.
mis.good: I was appalled by the quality.
mis.why: Use "appalling" for the thing and "appalled" for how you feel.

def: To show approval or praise by clapping, or express strong approval.
ex: Everyone applauded when the team announced zero downtime for six months.
nat: I applaud your decision to study every single morning.

mis.bad: We applauded to the speaker.
mis.good: We applauded the speaker.

def: Relevant or appropriate.
ex: This discount code is only applicable to annual subscriptions.
nat: Write N/A if a field on the form is not applicable to you.

mis.bad: This rule is applicable for everyone.
mis.good: This rule is applicable to everyone.

def: To assign a job or role to someone, or decide on a time/place.
ex: The board will appoint a new Chief Security Officer next month.
nat: They appointed Maria as head of engineering.

mis.bad: They appointed him like manager.
mis.good: They appointed him as manager / appointed him manager.

def: To assess the value or quality of someone or something.
ex: Managers appraise employee performance twice a year.
nat: An independent expert was hired to appraise the property.

mis.bad: We appraised about the house.
mis.good: We had the house appraised.
mis.why: "Appraise" is transitive; do not confuse with "apprise" (inform).

def: Anxious or fearful that something bad or unpleasant will happen.
ex: I felt a little apprehensive before my first presentation in English.
nat: Staff were apprehensive about the upcoming reorganization.

mis.bad: She was apprehensive with the flight.
mis.good: She was apprehensive about the flight.

def: Suitable or proper in the circumstances.
ex: Jeans and a clean shirt are completely appropriate for our office.
nat: Please choose an appropriate time to discuss the budget.

mis.bad: It is not appropriate to wear shorts for a wedding.
mis.good: Shorts are not appropriate for a wedding.
mis.why: Use "appropriate for [an occasion]" or "appropriate to + verb".

def: Close to the actual, but not completely accurate or exact.
ex: The approximate cost of the server upgrade is three hundred dollars a month.
nat: Can you give me an approximate arrival time?

mis.bad: The time is approximately about 20 minutes.
mis.good: The time is approximately 20 minutes.

def: Appropriate or suitable in the circumstances; or having a tendency to do something.
ex: "Premature optimization" is a very apt description of what happened here.
nat: Young children are apt to copy whatever adults say.

mis.bad: He is apt for making mistakes.
mis.good: He is apt to make mistakes.
mis.why: Use "apt to + base verb" for tendency.

def: Involving or requiring strenuous effort; difficult and tiring.
ex: Migrating five million rows without downtime was an arduous task.
nat: The hike to the summit was arduous, though the view made it worthwhile.

mis.bad: It was an arduous work.
mis.good: It was arduous work / an arduous job.
mis.why: "Work" is uncountable; do not use "an" before "arduous work".

def: To emerge; become apparent; or originate from a situation.
ex: Call me immediately if any unexpected issues arise during the deploy.
nat: Several questions arose after the security briefing.

mis.bad: A new error arised today.
mis.good: A new error arose today.

def: Made or produced by human beings rather than occurring naturally.
ex: Avoid foods full of artificial sweeteners and preservatives.
nat: Artificial intelligence is transforming customer support workflows.

mis.bad: The flowers are artificials.
mis.good: The flowers are artificial.
mis.why: Adjectives in English never take a plural "-s".

def: To go up or climb.
ex: The hikers began to ascend the steep ridge before sunrise.
nat: She quickly ascended to the position of Vice President.

mis.bad: We ascended up the hill.
mis.good: We ascended the hill.
mis.why: "Ascend" already means go up; never add "up".

def: To find something out for certain; make sure of.
ex: Tests help us ascertain whether the fix actually solved the memory leak.
nat: It was difficult to ascertain the exact cause of the fire.

mis.bad: Let us ascertain about the facts.
mis.good: Let us ascertain the facts.

def: To direct one's hopes or ambitions toward achieving something.
ex: Many junior developers aspire to lead their own engineering team someday.
nat: She aspired to become a fluent public speaker.

mis.bad: I aspire being a director.
mis.good: I aspire to be a director.
mis.why: Use "aspire to + noun" or "aspire to + base verb".

def: A physical attack, or a concerted attempt to do something demanding.
ex: The suspect was charged with assault outside the stadium.
nat: Stronger laws are needed to prevent online harassment and verbal assault.

mis.bad: He suffered an assault to his wallet (meaning robbery).
mis.good: He was robbed / mugged.
mis.why: "Assault" is a violent physical attack; theft of property is "robbery" or "theft".

def: To gather together in one place, or fit together the separate component parts of a machine.
ex: It took forty minutes to assemble the new office desk from the box.
nat: Staff were asked to assemble in the main hall at nine.

mis.bad: We assembled together at noon.
mis.good: We assembled at noon.

def: A useful or valuable thing, person, or quality; or property owned by a person or company.
ex: Speaking English comfortably is a huge career asset in global tech.
nat: Data security is one of a software company's most valuable assets.

mis.bad: Good communication is a big asset for us (plural mistake: assets).
mis.good: Good communication is a great asset.

def: To take in and understand information fully, or integrate into a wider society.
ex: Spaced review gives your brain time to assimilate new vocabulary naturally.
nat: Immigrants often work hard to assimilate into a new culture.

mis.bad: He assimilated well in the team.
mis.good: He assimilated well into the team.

def: To help someone, typically by doing a share of the work.
ex: Our support team is available twenty-four hours a day to assist customers.
nat: She assisted the lead architect in drafting the specification.

mis.bad: I assisted to the meeting (meaning attended).
mis.good: I attended the meeting.
mis.why: False friend! In English, "assist" means HELP, never "watch" or "attend".

def: To connect someone or something with something else in one's mind.
ex: Most users immediately associate green checkmarks with success.
nat: I would never associate him with reckless behavior.

mis.bad: People associate Brazil to football.
mis.good: People associate Brazil with football.
mis.why: Always use "associate A with B", never "to".

def: To surprise or impress someone greatly.
ex: It never fails to astonish me how fast babies pick up language sounds.
nat: Her calm performance astonished the entire jury.

mis.bad: I was astonishing by the result.
mis.good: I was astonished by the result.
mis.why: Use "-ed" for feelings ("astonished") and "-ing" for causes ("astonishing").

def: An effort to achieve or complete a difficult task or action.
ex: After three failed login attempts, the account locks for fifteen minutes.
nat: He passed his driving test on the very first attempt.

mis.bad: I made an attempt of fixing it.
mis.good: I made an attempt to fix it.
mis.why: Use "attempt to + base verb", not "attempt of + -ing".

def: To be present at an event or go regularly to a place; or to deal with something.
ex: All engineers are expected to attend Friday's architecture review.
nat: We have several urgent customer tickets to attend to today.

mis.bad: I will attend to the conference.
mis.good: I will attend the conference.
mis.why: Use "attend + event" with no "to"; "attend to" means deal with/take care of.

def: A settled way of thinking or feeling about something, reflected in behavior.
ex: A curious, patient attitude makes debugging far less frustrating.
nat: His positive attitude lifted the whole team's mood.

mis.bad: She has a good attitude with clients.
mis.good: She has a good attitude toward clients.

def: To regard something as being caused by someone or something.
ex: The team attributed the slowdown to an unindexed database table.
nat: Analysts attributed the drop in sales to seasonal demand.

mis.bad: They attributed the bug for a typo.
mis.good: They attributed the bug to a typo.

def: Able to be heard.
ex: There was a barely audible click before the microphone muted itself.
nat: Keep your voice loud enough to be audible at the back of the room.

mis.bad: The alarm was audible for listen.
mis.good: The alarm was clearly audible.

def: Of undisputed origin and not a copy; genuine.
ex: Listening to authentic podcasts exposes you to real rhythm and reductions.
nat: The restaurant serves authentic regional dishes from Oaxaca.

mis.bad: This watch is an authentic one original.
mis.good: This watch is authentic / an authentic piece.

def: The power or right to give orders and make decisions, or a person with deep knowledge.
ex: Only team leads have the authority to approve production database changes.
nat: She is a recognized authority on cryptography.

mis.bad: He is an authority in AI.
mis.good: He is an authority on AI.

def: Constituting the result obtained by adding quantities and dividing; or ordinary.
ex: The average response time stayed under eighty milliseconds all week.
nat: It was just an average Tuesday at the office.

mis.bad: In average, we spend 20 minutes.
mis.good: On average, we spend 20 minutes.

def: To turn away one's eyes or thoughts; or prevent an undesirable occurrence.
ex: Fast rollback alerts helped avert a major outage during peak traffic.
nat: She averted her eyes from the bright screen.

mis.bad: We averted to lose data.
mis.good: We averted data loss.
mis.why: "Avert" takes a noun object (a crisis, disaster), not "to + verb".

def: Having or showing a keen interest in or enthusiasm for something.
ex: He is an avid reader of science fiction and technical biographies.
nat: As an avid cyclist, she rides forty kilometers every Sunday.

mis.bad: She is avid for books.
mis.good: She is an avid reader.
mis.why: Usually placed directly before a noun ("avid reader/fan"), not with "for".

def: A painted cloth hung at the back of a theater stage, or the setting behind an event.
ex: The talks took place against a backdrop of rising energy prices.
nat: Snow-capped mountains formed a dramatic backdrop for the town.

mis.bad: In the backdrop of the city, you see hills.
mis.good: In the background of the photo, you see hills.
mis.why: Use "background" for photos/screens; use "backdrop" for figurative context or stage scenery.

def: To totally bewilder or perplex someone.
ex: The intermittent crash continued to baffle even the senior systems engineers.
nat: What baffles me is why nobody noticed the warning lights.

mis.bad: The bug baffled to everyone.
mis.good: The bug baffled everyone.

def: An even distribution of weight or elements; or the amount of money in an account.
ex: Finding a healthy balance between work and rest prevents burnout.
nat: Please check your account balance before scheduling the transfer.

mis.bad: I need to do a balance between study and rest.
mis.good: I need to strike a balance between study and rest.
mis.why: Natural collocation: "strike/find a balance", not "do a balance".

def: To send someone away from a country as punishment, or get rid of a feeling or thought.
ex: A ten-minute brisk walk is often enough to banish afternoon sleepiness.
nat: Try to banish the fear of sounding imperfect when you speak.

mis.bad: She banished the idea out of her mind.
mis.good: She banished the idea from her mind.

def: A fence or obstacle that prevents movement or access.
ex: Lack of confidence is often a bigger barrier than lack of vocabulary.
nat: Language barriers slowed down coordination between the two offices.

mis.bad: There is a barrier against learning.
mis.good: There is a barrier to learning.

def: The underlying support or foundation for an idea, argument, or process.
ex: Reviews are scheduled on a daily basis based on your memory curve.
nat: There is no factual basis for that rumor.

mis.bad: On a daily base, I read English.
mis.good: On a daily basis, I read English.

def: To endure an ordeal or difficulty; to carry or support weight or responsibility.
ex: Customers should not have to bear the cost of a vendor's billing error.
nat: I cannot bear listening to loud chewing during meetings.

mis.bad: Bear on mind that the deadline is Friday.
mis.good: Bear in mind that the deadline is Friday.
mis.why: The idiom is "bear in mind", never "on mind".

def: Very strange or unusual, especially so as to cause interest or amusement.
ex: It was bizarre that the bug only appeared on Tuesdays at midnight.
nat: The movie had a bizarre ending that left everyone confused.

mis.bad: That was a bizarrely incident.
mis.good: That was a bizarre incident.

def: Done openly and unashamedly; completely obvious (of bad behavior).
ex: Ignoring user consent banners is a blatant violation of privacy laws.
nat: The referee missed a blatant foul right in front of him.

mis.bad: He gave a blatant help.
mis.good: He made a blatant error / told a blatant lie.
mis.why: "Blatant" is used almost exclusively for negative things (lies, errors, violations).

def: To mix a substance with another so that they combine together seamlessly.
ex: The app tries to blend short spaced reviews with real reading practice.
nat: Oil and water do not naturally blend.

mis.bad: Blend the two styles between them.
mis.good: Blend the two styles together.
mis.why: Use "blend A and B" or "blend in with".

def: Showing an ability to take risks; confident and courageous.
ex: Switching careers into cybersecurity at thirty-five was a bold move.
nat: Highlight the deadline in bold so nobody misses it.

mis.bad: Put the title with bold.
mis.good: Put the title in bold.

def: To help or encourage something to increase or improve.
ex: Hearing native speakers every morning will boost your listening confidence.
nat: A quick walk after lunch always boosts my energy.

mis.bad: This will boost up our speed.
mis.good: This will boost our speed.

pt: destinado a / obrigado / com destino a
def: Walk or travel toward; certain to happen; or legally obliged.
ex: If we skip automated tests, bugs are bound to slip into production.
nat: This train is bound for Edinburgh.

mis.bad: It is bound that it fails.
mis.good: It is bound to fail.
mis.why: Always use "bound to + base verb", not "bound that...".
